opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it started with curiosity more than any grand plan. When I got to college, I was already the kind of person who liked poking at systems to see how they actually worked underneath, not just how they were supposed to work. Security was the field where that instinct was rewarded. You'd look at a program and ask, "What happens if I give it something nobody expected?" And sometimes the answer was that the whole thing fell apart, and you learned more from that moment than from reading the documentation.

There was also the competitive side. CTF competitions were really popular among students, and they're addictive. You get a binary or a web service, a clock is ticking, and you and your teammates are trying to find the flaw before anyone else. It felt like a puzzle game, except the puzzles were real software. It taught me reverse engineering, low-level debugging, reading assembly, and thinking about edge cases, skills that turned out to be useful far beyond security.

And I liked that it was very hands-on. You couldn't bluff your way through. Either your exploit worked or it didn't. That kind of immediate, honest feedback was really appealing to me as a student. Looking back, I think that mindset carried over into everything I did later, including machine learning infrastructure. You're still asking how the system really behaves, where it breaks, and how to make it robust.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started with curiosity more than any grand plan. I was in my first year at Tsinghua, and a few classmates were doing CTF competitions on weekends. I went along mostly because they were fun to be around, and I remember staring at a binary exploitation challenge for about six hours straight before it finally worked. That feeling of taking a system apart, understanding exactly why it behaves the way it does, and then making it do something its designers never intended, that completely hooked me.

What kept me there was realizing that security is really about understanding systems at every layer. You can't attack or defend something you don't deeply understand, so you end up learning operating systems, networking, compilers, cryptography, all of it, because you have to. For a student who liked building things, that was a great excuse to learn everything at once.

And then there was a competitive, team-oriented side to it. In CTFs you win or lose with your teammates in real time, and that taught me a lot about how to collaborate under pressure, which turned out to matter more later than any specific exploit technique I picked up.

Cybersecurity gave me a way to explore those questions while doing something useful—helping protect people and the information they rely on.
